items.title: 25.4 Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Drug Designing

source_refs.note: Topic 25.4 with the vitamin B12 box (PDF 142); the halicin structure is redrawn and the petri-dish photographs (Figure 25.5) are described. The exercises (PDF 143-144) are not part of the lesson body.

blocks.text: In the past few decades very few new antibiotics have been developed, and those that have are only slightly different from existing ones. Current methods of developing new drugs are very costly and time-consuming and usually explore a narrow range of chemical activity. At the same time, more and more infections resist existing antibiotics.

To find a solution, researchers at MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) designed a machine-learning model to look for the chemical features that make molecules effective at killing E. coli bacteria. They trained it on about 2500 molecules, including a set of 800 natural products with different structures and a wide range of activities. Applied to a large collection of compounds, the model picked out one molecule predicted to be antibacterial but with a structure different from existing antibiotics. A different model predicted that it would most likely have low toxicity to human cells. The molecule was named halicin and was tested against bacterial strains taken from patients: it killed many of the world's most problematic disease-causing bacteria that had resisted treatment.

After identifying halicin, the researchers used their model to screen more than 100 million molecules from a database in only three days. It selected 23 more molecules with structures different from existing antibiotics; eight of them showed antibacterial activity and two were particularly powerful. This work points to a new route for discovering organic molecules that may be used as drugs.

blocks.alt: The structure of halicin: an amino-1,3,4-thiadiazole ring (H2N on the left, S at the top, N-N at the bottom) joined through a sulfur atom to a 5-nitrothiazole ring (S at the top, N at the bottom, NO2 on the right). Below, five boxes: train a model on about 2500 molecules; it predicts which kill E. coli; halicin picked out, a new structure; screen over 100 million molecules in 3 days; 23 candidates, 8 active, 2 very powerful.
blocks.caption: Halicin and how artificial intelligence found it (original diagram for this topic).
blocks.long_description: Halicin contains two five-membered rings containing sulfur and nitrogen, joined by a sulfur atom, which is unlike any known antibiotic. The model learned from known molecules which features kill bacteria and then searched very large collections far faster than laboratory testing could.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: The book notes that the total synthesis of vitamin B12 was achieved by R. B. Woodward and A. Eschenmoser in 1972 after more than 10 years of collaboration; it involved over 100 steps, 91 post-doctoral researchers and 12 PhD students.

blocks.prompt: What did the AI model do that would have been very slow by laboratory testing?
blocks.explanation: It predicted the antibacterial activity (and likely toxicity) of very large numbers of molecules, screening over 100 million in three days and picking out a few candidates such as halicin for laboratory tests.

items: Few new antibiotics; resistance is growing.
An MIT machine-learning model found halicin, which kills resistant bacteria.
Screening over 100 million molecules in 3 days gave 23 candidates, 8 active.
